There's a flaw here. There IS an achievable maximum bandwidth, especially if your node is heavily subscribed. Will we hit this in normal use? No. But, I live in Indianapolis. Every year, my downstream drops from 95 ish megabits to under 2 during the indy500 race. But then, everyone in the loop has at least one, likely 3 or 4 devices all streaming HD at once, on top of normal traffic from people like me, who don't give a shit. However, let's take that situation. It doesn't cost Comcast any more or less to send me bit number 50 of the month than it will cost to send me bit number 50 trillion, and the events that can bring the network to its knees are few and far between; I don't notice this type of slowdown during the super bowl, for instance.

If we had more competition they'd be more likely to upgrade their equipment and buy/provision more waves on the backbone & last mile. Yes, there is a theoritical limit - but many of today's issues are caused by them not keeping up (despite being handed money by the government to do things such as that).

Hell, these bastards require payment for peering! Nobody but the biggest assholes do that. Basically, that makes it so not only are you paying to have them send data to you, but the upstream (usually originating) network is also paying them for the "privilege" of sending that data to you.
